mstress.rct_balance.pass: No evidence that the covariates jointly predict treatment (HC1 Wald test, p = {p:.3f}): consistent with randomization.
mstress.rct_balance.warning: The covariates jointly predict treatment (HC1 Wald test, p = {p:.3f}): randomization may have failed or been compromised.
mstress.rct_balance.no_covariates: No covariates: randomization balance cannot be checked.
mstress.rct_arm_size.pass: The smallest arm has {n} units (at least {minimum}).
mstress.rct_arm_size.warning: The smallest arm has only {n} units (fewer than {minimum}): robust standard errors are unreliable in samples this small.
mstress.matching_overlap.pass: {n} treated units ({share:.1%}) lie outside the control propensity range (at most {limit:.0%}).
mstress.matching_overlap.warning: {n} treated units ({share:.1%}) lie outside the control propensity range (more than {limit:.0%}): their matches are extrapolations.
mstress.matching_balance.pass: After matching every standardized difference is at most {limit} (largest {smd:.3f}).
mstress.matching_balance.warning: After matching a standardized difference of {smd:.3f} remains (above {limit}): the matches are not comparable on that covariate.
mstress.matching_extreme_ps.pass: {share:.1%} of propensity scores are beyond {cut} or below 1 - {cut} (at most {limit:.0%}).
mstress.matching_extreme_ps.warning: {share:.1%} of propensity scores are beyond {cut} or below 1 - {cut} (more than {limit:.0%}): weak overlap, and IPW weights become extreme.
mstress.matching_ipw_agreement.pass: Matching ({matching:.3f}) and IPW ({ipw:.3f}) do not differ significantly (p = {p:.3f}).
mstress.matching_ipw_agreement.warning: Matching ({matching:.3f}) and IPW ({ipw:.3f}) disagree (p = {p:.3f}): the estimate depends on the model of selection.
mstress.matching_ipw_agreement.na: The IPW standard error could not be bootstrapped: no comparison.
mstress.iv_weak_instrument.pass: First-stage F = {f:.1f}, above the rule-of-thumb threshold of {threshold:.0f} for weak instruments (Staiger & Stock, 1997).
mstress.iv_weak_instrument.warning: First-stage F = {f:.1f} (below {threshold:.0f}): weak instrument; 2SLS is biased towards OLS and its CI is unreliable.
mstress.iv_overidentification.pass: No evidence against the overidentifying restrictions (robust test, {df} restrictions, p = {p:.3f}). This cannot show that the instruments are valid: if all are invalid in the same way, the test does not detect it.
mstress.iv_overidentification.warning: The instruments disagree (robust overidentification test, {df} restrictions, p = {p:.3f}): at least one may violate the exclusion restriction.
mstress.iv_overidentification.just_ident: One instrument per endogenous variable: overidentification cannot be tested.
mstress.rdd_manipulation.pass: No significant difference between the counts just below and above the cutoff ({below} vs. {above}, p = {p:.3f}): no sign of manipulation of the running variable.
mstress.rdd_manipulation.warning: Counts just below and above the cutoff differ ({below} vs. {above}, p = {p:.3f}): units may sort around the cutoff.
mstress.rdd_manipulation.na: No observations near the cutoff: manipulation cannot be checked.
mstress.rdd_bandwidth.pass: The estimate does not change significantly when the bandwidth is halved ({half:.3f}) or doubled ({double:.3f}) (Hausman-type test, p = {p:.3f}).
mstress.rdd_bandwidth.warning: The estimate changes when the bandwidth is halved ({half:.3f}) or doubled ({double:.3f}) (Hausman-type test, p = {p:.3f}): the local linear fit may be biased by curvature.
mstress.rdd_bandwidth.na: The estimate could not be computed at half or double the bandwidth.
mstress.rdd_placebo_cutoffs.pass: No significant jump at the placebo cutoffs (median of the running variable on each side; Bonferroni p = {p:.3f} over {k}).
mstress.rdd_placebo_cutoffs.warning: A jump appears at a placebo cutoff (Bonferroni p = {p:.3f} over {k}): the outcome may be discontinuous for other reasons.
mstress.rdd_placebo_cutoffs.na: Too few observations on either side for placebo cutoffs.
mstress.sc_pre_fit.pass: Pre-treatment RMSPE {rmspe:.3f} is at most half the outcome's standard deviation ({sd:.3f}): good fit.
mstress.sc_pre_fit.warning: Pre-treatment RMSPE {rmspe:.3f} exceeds half the outcome's standard deviation ({sd:.3f}): the synthetic control does not reproduce the treated unit.
mstress.sc_leave_one_out.pass: Without the main donor {donor} (weight {weight:.2f}) the estimate is {estimate:.3f}, a change of {change:.2f} pre-period RMSPE.
mstress.sc_leave_one_out.warning: Without the main donor {donor} (weight {weight:.2f}) the estimate becomes {estimate:.3f}, a change of {change:.2f} pre-period RMSPE (more than 2): the result rests on one donor.
mstress.sc_leave_one_out.na: The estimate cannot be recomputed without the main donor (too few donors).
mstress.sc_in_time_placebo.pass: A fake treatment in period {period} shows no significant effect ({effect:.3f}, placebo p = {p:.3f}).
mstress.sc_in_time_placebo.warning: A fake treatment in period {period} shows an effect ({effect:.3f}, placebo p = {p:.3f} below 0.05): the method finds effects where there are none.
mstress.sc_in_time_placebo.na: Fewer than 4 pre-treatment periods: no in-time placebo.
mstress.dml_overlap.pass: The covariates explain {r2:.1%} of the treatment's variance (at most {limit:.0%}).
mstress.dml_overlap.warning: The covariates explain {r2:.1%} of the treatment's variance (more than {limit:.0%}): little treatment variation is left to identify the effect.
mstress.dml_seed_stability.pass: Another sample split gives {second:.3f} (vs. {first:.3f}), a shift of {shift:.2f} SE.
mstress.dml_seed_stability.warning: Another sample split gives {second:.3f} (vs. {first:.3f}), a shift of {shift:.2f} SE (more than 0.75): the result depends on how the folds are drawn.
methods.mc_intro: Draws the virtual world again with seeds {seed}, {seed} + 1, ... and runs the estimator on each, to measure its bias, precision and CI coverage under these settings.
methods.mc_only_virtual: The Monte Carlo needs a virtual world (known true effect).
methods.code_caption: Reproduces this estimate with the reference packages Causal Lab is tested against.
err.mc_reps: The Monte Carlo needs at least 2 replications (got {value}).
err.mc_failed: The estimator refused {failed} of {reps} replications: too few results for a Monte Carlo summary.
gen.nested_fe: Small-sample correction as in Stata xtreg, fe / reghdfe and R fixest: the unit dummies, nested in the clusters, are not counted (Causal Lab does the same).
gen.m.status.exact: Gives the same estimate and standard error as Causal Lab (checked by running this script).
gen.m.status.sc: Gives Causal Lab's estimate to within 0.01% (another optimizer for the same weights).
gen.m.status.close: Close to Causal Lab's estimate (within 0.1%), not identical: Synth's optimizer differs.
gen.m.status.differs: Not identical to Causal Lab: R's ranger forests and fold draws differ from scikit-learn's, so the estimate can move by about one standard error.
gen.m.status.unchecked: Not checked by Causal Lab (no Stata available): the options mirror Causal Lab's, differences are possible.
gen.m.conventional_row: Causal Lab reports the Conventional row
note.rdd_inference_robust: Robust bias-corrected inference (Calonico et al., 2014): the CI is centred on the bias-corrected estimate and accounts for the bias estimate; the point estimate shown is the conventional one.
estimand.rdd_fuzzy: Effect at the cutoff for compliers (fuzzy RD)
err.rdd_no_first_stage: The treatment does not jump at the cutoff: a fuzzy RD needs a first stage.
warn.rdd_weak_first_stage: Weak first stage at the cutoff (F = {f:.1f}, below {threshold:.0f}): the fuzzy RD estimate is unreliable.
summary.rdd.robust: Robust bias-corrected: estimate {estimate:.4f}, SE {se:.4f}, 95% CI [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}] (bias bandwidth b = {b:.4f})
summary.rdd.first_stage: First stage: jump in treatment {jump:.4f} (SE {se:.4f}, F = {f:.1f})
err.rdd_compliance: Compliance must be above 0 and at most 1 (got {value}).
methods.rdd_robust_caption: Robust bias-corrected (Calonico et al., 2014): bias-corrected estimate {estimate:.4f}, SE {se:.4f}, 95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}], p = {p:.3f}.
methods.rdd_first_stage_caption: Fuzzy RD first stage: the treatment jumps by {jump:.3f} at the cutoff (SE {se:.3f}, F = {f:.1f}).
methods.sc_predictors_caption: With predictors, the donor weights match these pre-treatment means, each weighted by its importance V, chosen to minimise the pre-treatment outcome error (Abadie et al., 2010). V is found by a local search: another optimizer can find a different V and different weights.
gen.m.status.sc_v: Close to Causal Lab's estimate, not identical: with predictors, the importance V is found by a local search, and this package's optimizer can stop at another V.
sources.title: External Data
sources.intro: Fetch public data into Causal Lab: DHS health and demographic indicators, WorldPop population by administrative unit, and ACLED conflict events (with your own ACLED account). Each dataset can be downloaded as CSV or sent to a Causal Methods page.
sources.disabled: The data connectors are off: Causal Lab sends nothing over the network. Turn them on in Settings to use this page.
sources.network_note: The connectors send requests to the services below: country codes, indicator ids, administrative boundaries, years, and for ACLED your e-mail and password (to ACLED only, never stored). No dataset loaded in Causal Lab is sent.

sources.dhs.countries: DHS country codes, comma-separated (e.g. CD, RW)
sources.dhs.unbalanced: Regions follow each survey's own boundaries, which change over time: a regional panel is usually unbalanced.

sources.worldpop.time: One request per unit and year: about {seconds:.0f} s per unit with these years.

err.worldpop_reply: WorldPop could not compute the population ({detail}).
err.acled_credentials: ACLED needs your account e-mail and password, and rejected the ones given.

err.acled_no_events: ACLED returned no events for this country and these years.
matrix.editor_hint: Type each player's payoffs below, one cell per pair of actions (at most {maximum} actions each).
matrix.n_equilibria: {n} equilibria (extreme points of each equilibrium set).
matrix.method_note: All equilibria by vertex enumeration of the best-response polytopes (as Gambit's enummixed); identical to Gambit on 800 test games. In a degenerate game, a set of equilibria is shown by its extreme points.
matrix.qre_intro: Players choose each action with probability proportional to exp(λ × its expected payoff): λ = 0 is random play, large λ approaches a Nash equilibrium (McKelvey & Palfrey, 1995). The curves follow the branch that starts from random play.
matrix.qre_branch_note: In games with a symmetry (Battle of the Sexes, Hawk-Dove) the branch splits; Causal Lab follows the symmetric continuation, where Gambit's path follower takes one side. Both are quantal response equilibria; on generic games the two agree to 1e-9.
matrix.prisoners_dilemma.name: Prisoner's dilemma
matrix.prisoners_dilemma.description: Each player gains by defecting whatever the other does, so both defect, although both would be better off cooperating.
matrix.matching_pennies.name: Matching pennies
matrix.matching_pennies.description: One player wants to match, the other to mismatch: no pure equilibrium; both randomize 50/50.
matrix.battle_of_sexes.name: Battle of the sexes
matrix.battle_of_sexes.description: Both want to coordinate but prefer different outcomes: two pure equilibria and one mixed.
matrix.hawk_dove.name: Hawk-Dove (chicken)
matrix.hawk_dove.description: Fighting is costly if both fight: one backs down in each pure equilibrium; in the mixed one both fight with probability 2/3.
matrix.stag_hunt.name: Stag hunt
matrix.stag_hunt.description: Cooperating pays only if the other cooperates too: a risky efficient equilibrium and a safe one.
matrix.inspection.name: Tax inspection game
matrix.inspection.description: A taxpayer chooses to comply (tax 1) or evade (fine 3 if caught); the authority chooses to inspect (cost 0.5) or not. Only a mixed equilibrium exists: a higher fine lowers inspections, not evasion (Tsebelis, 1989).
matrix.rock_paper_scissors.name: Rock-paper-scissors
matrix.rock_paper_scissors.description: Each action beats one and loses to another: the only equilibrium is to play each with probability 1/3.
err.matrix_shape: Each payoff matrix needs {rows} rows and {cols} columns.
err.matrix_size: Matrix games can have 1 to {maximum} actions per player.
err.matrix_finite: Every payoff must be a finite number.
err.qre_lambda: λ must be zero or positive (got {value}).
err.qre_path: The quantal response path could not be followed to λ = {value} (stopped at {reached:.3f}).
seq.stackelberg_intro: One agent, the leader, moves first; the others see its choice and play a Nash equilibrium among themselves. The leader anticipates that response (subgame-perfect equilibrium). The result is compared with the simultaneous game.
seq.first_mover: Moving first changes {leader}'s utility by {gain:+.4f} compared with the simultaneous game.
seq.stackelberg_method: For each leader strategy the followers' game is re-solved (warm-started, so it stays on one equilibrium branch); the leader's best strategy is found on a grid refined by a bounded search, and checked on a finer grid. Matches the closed forms of Cournot, Bertrand and Tullock leadership.
seq.nbs_intro: Two players split a surplus S. The Nash solution maximizes (u1 - d1)^α (u2 - d2)^(1-α): α is player 1's bargaining power, d1 and d2 what each gets if talks fail, u1 and u2 their utility of an amount m (e.g. m, or sqrt(m) for a risk-averse player).
seq.u1: Player 1's utility of an amount m
seq.u2: Player 2's utility of an amount m
seq.rubinstein_intro: Player 1 proposes a split; if player 2 refuses, player 2 proposes next period, and so on. Waiting costs each player its discount factor δ. The unique subgame-perfect equilibrium is immediate agreement; the chart shows player 1's share when only T offers can be made, and its infinite-horizon limit.
seq.brw: With short periods, this split is the Nash solution with bargaining power α = log δ2 / (log δ1 + log δ2) = {power:.3f}, which gives {nbs:.4f} (Rubinstein: {share:.4f}; Binmore et al., 1986).
err.stackelberg_agents: A Stackelberg game needs at least two agents.
err.stackelberg_leader: There is no agent {index} to lead.
err.stackelberg_no_response: The followers have no equilibrium response to any leader strategy.
err.bargain_alpha: The bargaining power must be strictly between 0 and 1.
err.bargain_no_gain: No split gives both players more than their disagreement payoff.
err.bargain_delta: Discount factors must be at least 0 and below 1.
err.bargain_rounds: There must be at least one offer.
md.intro: Each agent chooses several variables at once: a party's position on two issues, a firm's sales in two markets, a contestant's effort on two prizes. An equilibrium is a profile where no agent gains by changing any combination of its own variables.
md.editor_intro: List each agent's variables separated by commas (e.g. x, y). Bounds: one value for all variables, or one per variable in the same order.
md.solving: Solving best responses over every agent's variables...
md.method: Each best response is found on a grid over the agent's box, refined by L-BFGS-B with the exact gradient; best responses are iterated from several starting points, and the first-order conditions are then solved by Newton's method. A profile is shown only if no agent gains more than 1e-6 (relative) by deviating anywhere in its box. Matches the closed forms of the three catalogue models.
model.md_voting.name: Probabilistic voting on two issues
model.md_voting.description: Two parties choose a position on two issues. A voter of group g prefers positions close to its ideal point, weighting issue 2 by s, and votes for party A with a logit probability that rises with its advantage over B, at rate φ_g. Both parties converge to the mean of the ideal points weighted by group size × responsiveness, on each issue and whatever the weight s.
model.md_cournot.name: Multimarket Cournot ({n} firms)
model.md_cournot.description: Firms choose quantities in two markets. A joint production cost g/2 (q1 + q2)² links the markets: selling more in one raises the cost of the other, so a demand change in market 1 moves quantities in market 2. When market 2 is unprofitable enough, firms leave it (corner equilibrium).
model.md_contest.name: Contest over two prizes ({n} contestants)
model.md_contest.description: Contestants split effort between two Tullock prizes and pay c/2 times the square of their total effort. Effort on each prize is proportional to its value; a higher effort cost lowers both.
catalogue.md_voting: Public choice — Probabilistic voting on two issues
catalogue.md_contest: Public choice — Contest over two prizes
err.vector_agents: A game needs between 1 and {max} agents.
err.vector_bounds_count: {agent} has {n} variables: give one bound for all, or one per variable.
est.qre_intro: Given how often each action was chosen, find the logit QRE that makes these choices most likely (maximum likelihood). λ measures how strongly players respond to payoffs: 0 is random play, large λ is close to Nash equilibrium.
est.counts_of: Times each action of {player} was chosen
est.no_dataset: No dataset is loaded. Load one in the Virtual Lab or a Causal Methods page, or type the counts.
est.ignored_choices: {n} values do not match an action name and were ignored.
est.qre_at_bound: The likelihood keeps rising up to the end of the traced branch: choices are consistent with Nash equilibrium play and λ has no finite estimate. Only the lower bound of the confidence interval is informative.
est.qre_vs_random: Likelihood-ratio test against random play (λ = 0): LR = {lr:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}, from {n} observed choices.
est.qre_method: The likelihood is computed along the QRE principal branch, from λ = 0, and its maximum is refined by a bounded search (as Gambit's logit_estimate; equal to it to 1e-4 on 38 random games). Standard error from the curvature of the log-likelihood; the interval inverts the likelihood-ratio test, which stays valid near λ = 0 or when the likelihood is flat.
est.gmm_intro: Estimate the model's parameters from data in which each row is one observed equilibrium (for example one market). At the true parameters, each agent's first-order condition equals an unobserved shock that is uncorrelated with the instruments; GMM picks the parameters that make these correlations closest to zero. The equilibrium is never re-solved: only the observed strategies enter.
est.gmm_not_smooth: This model has no first-order conditions (its utilities are not smooth), so it cannot be estimated this way.
est.gmm_need_data: Choose a dataset with one row per observed equilibrium.
est.no_numeric: The dataset has no numeric column.
est.not_converged: The optimizer did not report convergence: try other starting values.
est.gmm_sample: {n} rows used ({dropped} with missing values dropped), {moments} moment conditions.
est.j_exact: As many moment conditions as parameters: the model is exactly identified and cannot be tested by overidentification.
est.j_reject: Hansen's J test rejects the moment conditions (J = {j:.2f}, df = {df}, p = {p:.4f}): the model, or an instrument's exogeneity, is contradicted by the data.
est.j_ok: Hansen's J test does not reject the moment conditions (J = {j:.2f}, df = {df}, p = {p:.4f}).
est.gmm_method: Two-step efficient GMM: first step weighted by the instruments' cross-products, second step by the inverse covariance of the moments; heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Equal to linearmodels' IV-GMM when the conditions are linear in the parameters; checked by simulation for a nonlinear model.
err.qre_counts_shape: Give one count per action: {rows} for the row player and {cols} for the column player.
err.qre_counts: Counts must be finite and not negative.
err.gmm_column: Column {column} is not in the dataset.
err.gmm_not_smooth: The model's utilities are not smooth: it has no first-order conditions to estimate from.
err.gmm_no_agent: Use at least one agent's first-order condition.
err.gmm_nothing: Choose at least one parameter to estimate.
err.gmm_role_twice: A parameter can have only one role: {names}.
err.gmm_strategy_column: Choose a column for every strategy (missing: {names}).
err.gmm_underidentified: {moments} moment conditions cannot identify {parameters} parameters: add instruments or first-order conditions, or estimate fewer parameters.
err.gmm_too_few_rows: {n} complete rows are too few for {moments} moment conditions.
err.gmm_start: The first-order conditions cannot be evaluated at the starting values (division by zero or a negative power): change them.
err.gmm_collinear_instruments: The instruments are collinear (one is a combination of the others, or constant).
err.gmm_singular_moments: The moment conditions are linearly dependent in this data: remove a redundant instrument or condition.
err.gmm_not_identified: The parameters are not identified: the moment conditions do not change with some combination of them (for example two intercepts that only appear as a sum). Fix one of them.
virtual.dropped_incomplete: {n} rows with a missing unit, period or outcome Y were left out.
err.iv_too_few: IV needs more complete observations than estimated parameters: found {n}, need at least {minimum}.
mstress.rct_balance.too_few: Too few complete observations ({n}) to test balance on {k} covariate(s).
methods.failed: The estimator could not run on these data ({detail}). Check that the chosen columns vary and that enough rows are complete.
mapping.all_missing: {role}: column '{column}' has no values (every row is empty).
online.sidebar_note: Public online demo: files you upload are processed on the hosting server. For confidential data, run Causal Lab on your own computer.
online.settings_note: This is the public online demo, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. Files you upload are processed in memory on that server; Causal Lab writes nothing to disk. The host keeps its own server logs and, on this platform, sends Streamlit's usage statistics from your browser (this cannot be turned off online). For confidential data, install Causal Lab on your own computer (README, section 6): there, every computation stays on your machine and no usage statistics are sent.
online.connectors_note: Online, the connectors' requests, including your ACLED e-mail and password, pass through the hosting server before reaching the data services. Use Causal Lab on your own computer for credentials you want to keep private.
report.software_intro: The numbers in this report were computed with the software versions below. Every random draw (Virtual World, bootstrap, cross-fitting) uses a fixed seed, so re-running the analysis with the same data, settings and versions reproduces them.
app.author: Author: {name}
demo.title: Guided demonstration
demo.intro: Causal Lab's main claim, tested as in a methods paper: on data where the answer is known, does difference-in-differences recover it, and does the lab say when it cannot?
demo.question: **Question.** In which conditions does two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (DiD) recover the treatment effect, with 95% confidence intervals that cover it as often as they claim? When a threat to identification grows, how wrong does it get, and does the pre-trend test of Break My Design notice?
demo.design: **Design.** Each Virtual World has {units} units over {periods} periods; {share} of the units are treated from period {tp}, with a true effect of {att} and noise of standard deviation {sd}. Four threats are varied one at a time, each at five levels from *none* to *severe*: diverging pre-trends, confounding, staggered adoption with effects that grow over time, and anticipation (each tab below describes its threat exactly). In every world: the DiD estimate with standard errors clustered by unit, and the joint test of the pre-treatment leads with a wild cluster bootstrap p-value, which warns at the 10% level.
demo.one_world_caption: One draw each (seed {seed}): an illustration, not evidence. Section 3 repeats the experiment on a thousand worlds.
demo.no_study: The stored simulation study is missing. Run `python spike/demo_study.py` from the repository root.
demo.col.coverage_pass: Coverage when the test does not warn
demo.table_note: Monte Carlo standard errors in parentheses (Morris et al., 2019). Bias is the mean of the estimate minus the true effect. When the empirical SE (the spread of the estimates) and the mean model SE (what the estimator reports) agree, the reported uncertainty is honest.
demo.provenance: {reps} worlds per level and threat, seeds {seed} + r (r = 0, …, {reps} − 1), computed by `{script}` (last run {date}) and stored with every replication; the same seed r gives the same noise at every level and threat.
demo.reading_clean: **When parallel trends hold**, the 95% interval covers the true effect in {coverage} of the worlds (Monte Carlo SE {mcse}), the bias is {bias} (MCSE {bias_mcse}), and the effect is detected (H0: ATT = 0 rejected) in {rejection} of them. The pre-trend test warns in {false_alarm} of these worlds: its false-alarm rate, against a nominal 10%.
demo.reading_violated: **When they fail severely**, the estimator is biased by {bias}: the mean estimate is {mean} for a true effect of {att}, and in {wrong_sign} of the worlds the DiD reports a *significant effect of the wrong sign*. Its interval covers the truth in {coverage} of them. The pre-trend test warns in {detection} of these worlds; at the *{high_level}* level, in {high_detection}: a violation that reverses the conclusion can still go unnoticed.
demo.reading_pretest: **Passing the pre-trend test does not make the estimate trustworthy.** At the *{level}* level, {n_pass} of {reps} worlds pass the test, yet their intervals cover the true effect in only {coverage_pass} of them, against a nominal 95%. A passed test is an absence of evidence, not evidence of parallel trends; and estimating only after a passed pretest changes the distribution of the estimator (Roth, 2022).
demo.rerun_intro: The first worlds of a threat and level are drawn again with the same seeds and compared with the stored ones, value by value. Each world takes about a second on the free online server, a fraction of that on a laptop.
demo.rerun_result: {n} worlds re-run: coverage {coverage}, bias {bias}, the pre-trend test warns in {detection}.
demo.rerun_identical: Identical to the stored replications: the study is reproducible.
demo.rerun_differs: Differs from the stored replications: the software versions or the code have changed since the study was computed.
demo.ck_note: Each cell: published value (standard error) · Causal Lab's value (standard error), recomputed from the raw survey data. The last cell of the last row is the difference-in-differences: the change in employment in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania after New Jersey's minimum-wage increase.
demo.ck_agreement: **{agree} of {cells}** published numbers are reproduced to two decimals. The other is the standard error of NJ − PA after the increase: 1.08 from the data, 1.07 published. Combining the published cell standard errors, sqrt(0.52² + 0.94²) = 1.074, also gives 1.07: the gap is the rounding of those inputs, not a different estimate.
demo.limits:
- **The simulated worlds are simple.** One kind of violation at a time, with linear trends and normal noise. Real data can combine several threats, and depart from parallel trends in ways the lead test has little power against.
- **A passed test is not a proof.** The pre-trend test, like every check of Break My Design, can only find evidence against an assumption. The Identification Strength score summarises these checks; it is a heuristic, not a measure of validity.
- **A replication is not a validation of the design.** Reproducing Card & Krueger's numbers shows that the computation is right; whether their comparison identifies the causal effect is the subject of a later literature that this page does not settle.
demo.rule: **Decision rule: how much bias is too much.** The DiD is judged acceptable in a scenario when its bias is at most {share} of the true effect (|bias| ≤ {tolerance} here) **and** its 95% interval covers the true effect in at least {coverage} of the worlds. The author fixed this rule on 2026-10-30, after seeing the results for diverging pre-trends and before simulating the three other threats; it is recorded in the project's planning log.
demo.overview_title: How far can each threat go before the DiD goes wrong too much?
demo.threat.differential_trend.name: Diverging pre-trends
demo.threat.differential_trend.desc: Treated units drift away from the controls even without treatment, by 0.08 × intensity noise SDs per period, centred on the treatment date (intensity 0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.2 and 2.0 from none to severe). Parallel trends fail.
demo.threat.confounding.name: Confounding
demo.threat.confounding.desc: Units with a high value of a covariate X1 are more likely to be treated (logistic selection whose slope is the intensity), and X1 also shifts the trend of the outcome. X1 is not in the DiD model: the comparison group follows a different trend for a reason the model does not see.
demo.threat.staggered_dynamic.name: Staggered adoption, growing effects
demo.threat.staggered_dynamic.desc: Treated units adopt at different dates (periods 10 to 15), and each unit's effect grows, per period since its own adoption, by 25% × intensity of its base effect. Two-way fixed effects then use earlier adopters, whose effects are still growing, as controls for later ones (Goodman-Bacon, 2021). The true effect is the mean over treated unit-periods, so it grows with the level; the bias is judged relative to it.
demo.threat.anticipation.name: Anticipation
demo.threat.anticipation.desc: In the period just before its own adoption, a treated unit's outcome already moves by 0.5 × intensity noise SDs in the direction of the effect, while it is still recorded as untreated.
demo.reading_threat_bad: **Within the rule up to *{last}*.** At *{level}*, the bias is {bias} ({share} of the effect) and the interval covers the true effect in {coverage} of the worlds. The pre-trend test warns in {detection} of them, against {baseline} when there is no threat: what it detects here is the gap between the two.
demo.reading_threat_never: **Outside the rule from *{level}* on.** The bias is {bias} ({share} of the effect) and the interval covers the true effect in {coverage} of the worlds. The pre-trend test warns in {detection} of them, against {baseline} when there is no threat.
demo.reading_threat_all_ok: **Within the rule at every level.** Even at the severe level, the bias is {bias} ({share} of the effect) and the coverage {coverage}: in this design, the DiD withstands this threat.
demo.bias_dist_title: Distribution of the bias over the worlds

stress.pt.not_enough: Not enough pre-treatment periods or groups to test pre-trends.
stress.pt.too_few_units: Only {n} units: with fewer than {minimum}, the bootstrap test of pre-trends cannot reach the 10% level, so it is not run.
stress.pt.plausible: Parallel trends: plausible. No evidence of differential pre-treatment trends (p = {p:.3f}).
stress.pt.questionable: Parallel trends: questionable. The joint test of pre-treatment group-specific trends rejects equal trends (p = {p:.3f}); differential pre-trends threaten the parallel-trends assumption.
stress.pt.violated: Parallel trends: violated. The joint test of pre-treatment group-specific trends rejects equal trends (p = {p:.3f}); differential pre-trends threaten the parallel-trends assumption.
stress.anticipation.not_enough: Not enough data to test for anticipation effects.
stress.anticipation.warning: Outcome jumps for treated units in the period right before treatment (p = {p:.3f}), suggesting possible anticipation.
stress.anticipation.pass: No evidence of anticipatory behavior just before treatment (p = {p:.3f}).
stress.spillovers.non_numeric: Unit identifiers are not numeric, so no neighbourhood structure is available to test for spillovers.
stress.spillovers.no_neighbourhood: Unit identifiers of these data do not encode a neighbourhood (adjacent ids are not known to be neighbours), so spillovers to nearby controls cannot be tested here. Not counted in the score.
stress.spillovers.too_few: Too few adjacent / non-adjacent control units to test for spillovers. Not counted in the score.
stress.spillovers.warning: The {n} control unit(s) adjacent to a treated unit shift by {effect:+.3f} after treatment relative to other controls (p = {p:.3f}). Spillovers contaminate the comparison group.
stress.spillovers.pass: No significant difference after treatment between control units adjacent to a treated unit and the other controls (difference = {effect:+.3f}, p = {p:.3f}).
stress.serial.warning: Within-unit Durbin-Watson statistic = {dw:.2f}; implied residual autocorrelation (corrected for fixed-effects bias) = {rho:.2f}. Serially correlated errors make non-clustered standard errors too small (Bertrand et al., 2004): keep clustering by unit, and consider a wild-cluster bootstrap when clusters are few.
stress.serial.pass: Within-unit Durbin-Watson statistic = {dw:.2f}; implied residual autocorrelation (corrected for fixed-effects bias) = {rho:.2f}, no strong evidence of serial correlation.
stress.serial.not_enough: Serial correlation needs at least three periods; with two periods the within-unit residuals are mechanically opposite. Not counted in the score.
stress.heterogeneity.too_few: Too few treated or control units to assess effect heterogeneity. Not counted in the score.
stress.heterogeneity.warning: Pre/post changes vary more across treated units than across controls (variance ratio = {ratio:.2f}, p = {p:.3f}). A single average treatment effect may mask important heterogeneity.
stress.heterogeneity.pass: Pre/post changes are not significantly more dispersed across treated units than across controls (variance ratio = {ratio:.2f}, p = {p:.3f}).
rec.did.intro: Difference-in-Differences is potentially appropriate because treatment occurs at a defined point in time and the data contain treated and comparison units observed before and after the intervention.
rec.did.staggered: Treatment adoption is staggered: a standard two-way fixed-effects DiD estimate can be contaminated by already-treated units used as controls. A heterogeneity-robust estimator (Callaway & Sant'Anna, de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille) is recommended over the canonical TWFE specification.
rec.did.spillovers: Because nearby or related units may also be affected (spillovers), a Spatial Spillover Analysis extension is recommended alongside the baseline DiD.
rec.did.assumption: Parallel trends between treated and comparison units in the absence of treatment.
rec.event_study.intro: An Event Study is a natural extension of DiD: it estimates period-by-period treatment effects and lets you inspect pre-treatment coefficients directly as an informal test of the parallel-trends assumption.
rec.event_study.few_pre: Fewer than two pre-treatment periods are available, which limits the ability to visually or statistically assess pre-trends.
rec.event_study.assumption: No anticipation effects; parallel trends in each pre-treatment period.
rec.event_study.concern: Statistical power in periods far from the treatment date.
rec.synthetic_control.intro: Synthetic Control is most useful when a single (or very few) treated unit(s) can be compared against a weighted combination of untreated donor units that closely tracks its pre-treatment trajectory.
rec.synthetic_control.assumption: No interference between the treated unit and donor units; good pre-treatment fit.
rec.synthetic_control.concern: Inference relies on placebo-based permutation tests rather than standard errors.
rec.iv.intro: Instrumental Variables can address endogenous treatment assignment, but the score here is capped because no valid instrument has been declared in the current project — relevance and exclusion restriction cannot be assessed automatically.
rec.iv.assumption: Instrument relevance and exclusion restriction (no direct effect on the outcome).
rec.iv.concern: Weak instruments bias estimates toward the OLS estimate.
rec.rdd.matches: Regression Discontinuity is only appropriate when treatment is assigned by whether a running variable crosses a known cutoff. This design's assignment mechanism is '{mechanism}', which matches this requirement.
rec.rdd.no_match: Regression Discontinuity is only appropriate when treatment is assigned by whether a running variable crosses a known cutoff. This design's assignment mechanism is '{mechanism}', which does not obviously match this requirement.
rec.rdd.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable around the cutoff.
rec.rdd.concern: Local validity only: estimates apply near the cutoff, not to the full population.
rec.matching.intro: Matching / propensity-score methods require that, conditional on observed covariates, treatment assignment is as good as random (no unobserved confounding). This is a strong and untestable assumption.
rec.matching.concern: Unobserved confounding cannot be ruled out or tested directly.
rec.rct.declared: A Randomized Controlled Trial design was declared for this project.
rec.rct.not_declared: A Randomized Controlled Trial design was not declared for this project: treatment assignment is described as non-random, so an RCT-style analysis is not applicable retroactively. This score reflects that an RCT was not the assignment mechanism used.
diagnosis.note.staggered: Staggered treatment timing detected: standard two-way fixed-effects DiD can be biased under treatment-effect heterogeneity (Goodman-Bacon, 2021; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfœuille, 2020). Consider heterogeneity-robust DiD estimators.
diagnosis.note.endogenous_language: The research question mentions self-selection or reverse causality language; treat the assignment mechanism as potentially endogenous.
diagnosis.note.no_pre_periods: No pre-treatment periods are available: pre-trends and time-invariant confounding cannot be assessed directly.
diagnosis.note.spatial: Spatial or network language detected: treated and comparison units may not be independent (SUTVA violation). Consider a spillover / spatial-DiD analysis.

model.downs.name: Downsian median voter
model.downs.description: Two office-seeking parties choose platforms on a line; voters with single-peaked preferences vote for the closer platform. Both parties converge to the median voter's ideal point.
model.probabilistic_voting.name: Probabilistic voting
model.probabilistic_voting.description: Parties maximize expected vote share when voters' choices are subject to random ideological shocks. Policy converges to an average of group ideal points weighted by group size and responsiveness: responsive (swing) groups get more weight.
model.tullock.name: Tullock rent-seeking contest ({n} contestants)
model.tullock.description: Interest groups spend resources to win a politically allocated rent; each wins with probability proportional to its effort. With identical prizes each spends (n-1)V/n^2 and a share (n-1)/n of the rent is dissipated.
model.niskanen.name: Niskanen budget-maximizing bureau
model.niskanen.description: A bureau with a monopoly on supply maximizes its budget subject to covering its costs. When budget-constrained it produces twice the socially optimal output.
model.public_good.name: Voluntary public-good provision ({n} contributors)
model.public_good.description: Citizens split their income between private consumption and contributions to a public good. Free riding leads to under-provision; poorer citizens may not contribute at all.
model.cournot.name: Cournot oligopoly ({n} firms)
model.cournot.description: Firms choose quantities simultaneously facing linear inverse demand P = a - bQ.
model.bertrand.name: Bertrand duopoly with differentiated products
model.bertrand.description: Two firms set prices for imperfect substitutes with linear demands q_i = a - b p_i + d p_j.
param.downs.m: Median voter's ideal point (one-dimensional policy space)
param.tullock.prize: Value of the rent (prize) for contestant {i}
param.niskanen.a: Sponsor's marginal valuation at zero output
param.public_good.alpha: Weight on private consumption (1 - alpha on the public good)
